LEWIS (West Huron) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 66), to
amend the Railway Act. He said:	Mr. Speaker, the Bill which I wish to introduce is almost identical with the Bill which I introduced last year, with this exception, that I have added a clause providing that all railways doing business in Canada after the first of July, 1910, shall report to the Dominion government the names and employment of all men in their employ who work over 12 hours on any day, or an aggregate of 84 hours in any week. The Bill jirovides that this clause shall apply only to trainmen, des-patchers, operators, and any others who have anything to do with the management or running of trains. The object of this- and I believe it will be welcomed by the railways-is to assist in the prevention of a great many accidents which are due to the lengthy hours despatchers and others are sometimes employed. I have had a number of complaints from different men of the long hours they have to work: but you can readily understand that if these complaints were looked into by the railway authorities, the men who make the complaints might be militated against by their employers, whereas if the railways are obliged to make a report, that is public property. I feel much more strongly than I did'last year, that there should be a public official representing the people of Canada, not the railway corporations or the municipalities, but the man of moderate means who has a grievance which he wishes to lay before the Railway Commission and is not in a position to do so on his own behalf. Since I introduced the Bill of last year, a number of cases have been brought to my attention in which an official of that kind would have been of great service to the people of Canada. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will hand into 'Hansard' the remarks which I made in introducing the Bill of last session.

speechtext:
BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved second reading of Bill (No. 25) respecting the water carriage of goods. He said: The most important feature of the Bill is that concerning a clause which is to be found in many Bills of lading, providing that the ship owners will not be liable in cases of fault or negligence on their part. This contracting out of liability seems to me absolutely contrary to the principles of our laws. Some years ago we passed legislation preventing railway companies from doing this and declaring that any such clause would be considered illegal. I may say that similar legislation to the one we are now introducing has been passed in Australia and is also in force in the United .States, and the present Bill is taken mostly from the provisions of that passed by the Australian parliament. Some of its provisions are also in conformity with those of the Bill passed in the United States. True no such legislation exists in England, but the tendency at least in this country has been to disregard as much as possible the clauses in Bills of lading I have referred to. It ought not to be necessary for me to dwell at any length on the principle of the Bill. It is one which certainly ought to commend itself to the favourable consideration of this House. Let me draw attention to one of the clauses in the Bill of lading of a prominent shipping line:-
It is further expressly agreed that the goods named herein are shipped and carried at the sole risk of the shipper or owner thereof, and that the ship owner shall in no case be responsible for any loss or damage thereof, or in any wise relating thereto, whether such loss and damage arise, defects or insufficiency, either before or after shipment, in the hull of the said steamer, or in her machinery, or boilers or refrigerating chambers,- machinery or in any part of the refrigerating apparatus, or in any material, or the supply or use thereof used in the process of refrigeration, and whether such loss Mr. LEWIS.
or damage however arising, be caused by the negligence, default, error of judgment of the pilot, master, officers, engineers, mariners, refrigerating engineers, or other servants of the ship owner or persons for whom they are responsible or by negligence in stowage.
Here is another clause:-
Hook marks or injury from hooks, stowage or contact with or smell or evaporation from any other goods or from live stock or their excretion, however caused.
*
In this case it is provided also that there shall be no liability. It is provided also that if the goods should be delivered to some , other person than the ones mentioned as being those to whose order the goods should be delivered, there will be no liability. I may say, however, to the credit of the ship owners as a rule that they do not take advantage of those extraordinary provisions. But possibly in some cases some companies, not quite so reputable, might not fail to take advantage of them. And it is possible that a company, who would be absolutely responsible in ordinary cases for the negligence of its officers and servants, might contract itself out of any liability arising from such negligence. Therefore it seems to me that we should provide that such clauses in a Bill of lading should be absolute illegal. This is the law which exists in Australia and the United States. I might add that in the province of Quebec, there is in its Civil Code a proviso almost similar to the one I am now introducing. That provision has been working satisfactorily and is in accord also with section 284 of the Railway Act. That section says:-
The company, shall, according to its powers:
(b) Furnish adequate and suitable accommodation for the carrying, unloading and delivering of such traffic.
And subsection 7 of the same section says:
Every person aggrieved by any neglect or refusal of the company to comply with the requirements of this section, shall, subject to this Act, have an action therefor against the company, from wrhich action the company shall not be relieved by any notice, condition or declaration, if the damage arises from any negligence or omission of the company or of its servants.
Current jurisprudence also tends to declare that the responsibility for accidents, not only when negligence is established against the shipowner or carrier, but in other cases also is upon the carrier. That is, the onus probandi in such cases rests upon the person against whom the action in damages is taken. The general principle of law is that one is not responsible unless it be proven that the accident or damage is due to his thought, fault or negligence. But, while this principle may

have been, not only sound but applicable before the present industrial development, yet, under present conditions, as shown by cases recently decided by the Supreme Court, the onus probandi rests upon the person using the appliances which are the cause of the accident. For it is extremely difficult in ordinary cases for the person aggrieved to prove that the accident is due to the negligence of the carrier. The courts have been giving to that disposition of the law the most liberal interpretation and have held the carrier responsible, not only when negligence has been proven, but when the presumption of negligence has been more or less well established. Thus the tendency of the law is more and more in favour of holding responsible the persons or companies to whose care goods are entrusted for transportation. But, in the case of shipowners, the carriers go so far as to contract themselves out of their liability even for damages due to their own negligence or fault. This is certainly a step contrary to the ordinary principles of the law, ot, at least, of the jurisprudence that is now being established in this country. It seems necessary to guard against such contracts and to enact a provision to make it impossible for these parties^ to contract themselves out of these liabilities, and for that purpose to declare such conditions of the contract to be illegal. That is the main object of this Bill. I may say that a measure on this subject was introduced in the Senate two years ago and was fully discussed there. An opportunity was given for interested parties, shipowners and others, to be heard. The result of the Senate's deliberations was a Bill which is almost word for word the one now before the House. Last year this Bill was passed again by the Senate, but, unfortunately, it reached this House too late to be considered. I believe it came to us just at the end of the session, and, as some objection was taken to it, it could not be passed. This year, I thought I would take charge of the Bill and submit it to the favourable consideration of this House. I entirely agree with the work done by the Senate, and I am very glad to say that the work is a good guide for us in this case, and we could not do better than follow the principles which they accepted last year, and which I am sure they will accent this year also. The other day we received in the department a letter from a shipowner who asked to be heard on the subject of this Bill. I think it is only fair that an opportunity for hearing should be afforded to those interested, and with that view, if the Bill passes its second reading, I intend to propose that it be referred to the Committee on Marine and Fisheries for that purpose.

I desire to direct the attention of the Prime .Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to the very great delay in having the documents connected with the resignation of Mr. Lumsden laid before the House in printed form, and so made available for all the members. I repeat what I have already said in that regard-that, considering the importance of these documents, considering that they relate to a matter connected with the expenditure of $150,000,000, and $200,000,000, the government ought to have laid these documents in printed form upon the table of the House on the very first day of the session. Instead of that, there was delay until they could be moved for, and since they were moved for there has been the additional unnecessary delay of waiting for them to be printed while the House is sitting. I moved for the papers at once, and they w'ere ordered to be printed almost as soon as they were brought down. It is now a little more than four weeks since the session opened, and these papers are not yet available. The answer of the Prime Minister to representations on

this subject has been thairthe printing of these papers is within the power and control of this House. The House does not do its own printing, but resorts to a department of the government to have its printing done. The House has done all it could do in connection with the matter by ordering that the papers shall be printed. Yet most extraordinary and unusual delay has taken place so that we shall not have these documents available for any intelligent work until two months after the opening of the session. I think that that is a very regrettable state of affairs. If delays of this kind unnecessarily prolong the session upon which we have entered, I desire to say in advance that it is not the fault of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, but it is the fault of those who are responsible for the administration of affairs, and who have lamentably failed in their duty in that regard.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY-IMPURE WATER ON PASSENGER TRAINS.
INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY-IMPURE WATER ON PASSENGER TRAINS.
speechtext:
Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) to the quality of the water supplied ' to the Intercolonial railway at Montreal, which is dangerous to the life and health of passengers travelling on its trains. Montreal is suffering from a very severe epidemic of typhoid fever, and the water supply of the city is without doubt, and is acknowledged to be, a source of danger. The milk of that city is also said to be contaminated, and the contamination may properly be traced to the water. In travelling on that train I made inquiries in the dining caT, where the water came from, and I was told by those in charge that the water tank was filled from the water service of the city of Montreal. Now, if the citizens of Montreal are willing to put up with a municipal council that quenches their thirst on poisonous fluid, that is no reason why an innocent traveller on the Intercolonial should suffer in his health or in his life from this contaminated water. 1 am not talking of unrealities, but of a sad and actual reality. Many cases of typhoid have been contracted in this way from the impure water served to travellers. The Intercolonial is not the only railway that has been asked to supply its passengers with harmless water, and there has been more than one case where an order to give pure water has not been fully complied with, and when it has been found-I am not now referring to the Intercolonial-that the dining cars were furnished with pure water, while the ordinary passengers' lavatories and washrooms were supplied with impure water. Now it is as dangerous for a man to clean his teeth with water Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
loaded with typhoid bacillus as it is to drink typhoid water. Many a man is carried to his death by merely having cleaned his teeth by water full of typhoid bacillus. A case of typhoid contracted on a railway between Montreal and Quebec or between Montreal and Hamilton may not develop for a week or two, perhaps in Cape Breton or perhaps in Vancouver, and the victim wonders where he contracted the typhoid. To show that I am not an alarmist, I want to read a quotation from Thursday's Montreal ' Star ':
The typhoid situation is now serious.
Hospitals are too full to accommodate all fever patients who apply.
The following is the record of cases at the leading hospitals to-day:-
Royal Victoria Hospital	 66
General Hospital	 46
Western Hospital	 20
Notre Dame	 22
Since this was published I find by the 1 Star ' of yesterday and the ' Star ' of today that the epidemic is growing worse and worse. People are told to boil the water. Well, that is a straw in catching at which many a man drowns. Drinking boiled water is safe, but eating off dishes and with spoons, knives and forks that have been washed with unboiled water, though the water may be warm, still renders one liable to contract the disease. I am not here pleading for the citizens of Montreal, they have put up with contaminated water for many years; but I am pleading for the unsuspecting traveller who, when he sees the innocent looking water supplied in the dining car, thinks he is drinking the pure fluid, whereas he is frequently drinking disease and in many cases death. This is an easy thing to remedy, and it is only a just thing to ask; and I am sure it will only be necessary to draw the attention of the Minister of Railways to this matter to have the danger removed so far as the Intercolonial is concerned. But I am sure a complete remedy will not be found unless there is a thorough investigation made and a thorough remedy applied, because the average railway servant and the average individual do not comprehend the danger of drinking typhoid water. I do not know that I have any right to complain on behalf of other railways, but there is no harm in drawing their attention to the fact that many of them are filling their tanks to supply their passengers with the vile water supply of Montreal.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext:
I desire to. offer for the consideration of the House an amendment to the motion to go into Supply. The amendment only affirms a principle laid down in the rules of the House which the House has followed in the past, and which it is well to conserve for future use. It will be remembered that on the first of the present month I called the attention of the hon. the First Minister to the position that he then and still holds in occupying the two seats of Quebec East and the city of Ottawa. I asked at that time for your ruling as to whether the right hon. gentleman, in continuing to hold the dual position as representative of these two seats, yas committing a breach of the rules of the House. The following day you ruled that the right hon. the First Minister was not committing such a breach of privilege. I am quite prepared to admit, as I do by the amendment in my hand, that so far as your ruling on that point is concerned, the House can not question it. I have no recourse and consequently I do not purpose by this amendment to reverse the ruling which was given by Mr. Speaker on the 2nd of December last. I desire, however, that my words in that regard shall not be misconstrued. I wish to state that I admit only that we are bound by the conclusion reached by Mr. Speaker in relation to this particular case/ I do not wish to be understood as saying that we are any further bound. We have concluded in the present case that the right hon. the First Minister is not committing a breach of privilege and therefore, by reason of the fact that we are so concluded by the rule of the House, I cannot now and do not now challenge that ruling. But, Sir, in the course of the reasoning by which you arrived at that conclusion, certain principles were stated which I think were erroneously stated, and which I think it is to the advantage of the House to reaffirm. In the course of that ruling it was stated, among other things, that sessional orders of the House of Commons of Great Britain and Ireland such as were in force on the 1st day of July, 1867, were not within the meaning of the word ' rules ' as used in Rule 1 of the House of Commons of Canada. That, I think, was an error and, to reaffirm what I said before, while we are concluded as to the application, correctly or incorrectly, of that rule in the present instance, we are in no way precluded from the use and enjoyment of the rule in time to come. That is to say,
while it may or may not be misconstrued in an individual case, it still is of use in this House and its reaffirmation under the present circumstances is advisable. I therefore feel that before going any further I should offer to the House the amendment to the motion for Supply which I propose to move. It is as follows:
That in the judgment of this House, sessional orders of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland in force on the first day of July, 1867, are within the meaning of the words ' rules, usages and forms of proceedings,' as contained in rule 1 of the rules of the House of Commons of Canada.
In supporting that amendment, I desire first of all to refer to the use of the word ' rules ' and the word ' orders ' in the standard authority of this House, Sir John Bourinot's work on parliamentary procedure. It will be found by a reference to Bourinot at pages 303-4-5-6 and 7, that the words ' rule ' and ' order ' are used practically interchangeably; no distinction is drawn between' them, sometimes the word ' rule ' is used, sometimes the word ' order,' each in reference to the same subject, each in denomination of the same distinctive idea. There is no distinction drawn, the one means the other, and the other means the one, in so far as they both are used to refer to regulations and proceedings in the House of Commons. I do not think it necessary to quote individual sentences from Bourinot. A reference to the pages I have cited will clearly show any member that no distinction is drawn between the two words.
Now then, is there any distinction under the English practice? I desire in this case to be more specific, because fortunately the English authorities on this question are very clear, and I affirm that it is absolutely impossible for any hon. gentleman, approaching this subject in a reasonable attitude, to come to any other conclusion than that sessional orders and all orders that form the basis of procedure, or the regulation of procedure, are included within the meaning of the word ' rules.' I refer now to Redlich on the procedure of the House of Commons, volume 2, at page 5, and I regret that in order to make myself perfectly clear it will be necessary for me to read a considerable part of what that authority says on this subject. Perhaps, that it may be grasped more clearly, I should indicate the course of his reasoning. He urges that there are three classes of orders, all embraced within the meaning of the word ' rule.' There are, first of all, standing orders; secondly, sessional orders, and thirdly, another class which are not denominated correctly by either of the other terms and which are not given in their

promulgation in the first instance, either short or long duration. This third class of orders, it will be seen, are embraced within the meaning of the word ' rule.' In the opening of that argument Redlich draws a distinction between the word ' order ' as used in the specific instance in reference to a specific case and the word ' order ' as properly termed, a regulation which has an abstract reference. He says the word ' order ' is used in two senses. It might mean a concrete direction as to what is to be done in a particular case or it might describe an abstract formulation of a rule as to the business of the House. In the first sense, an order is the commonest act of the House of Commons, the motive power of all its actual, positive work. We have nothing to do with orders of the House in this sense, we are only concerned with orders which are abstract regulations. As to what orders are .abstract regulations, he says:
The mark which distinguishes orders of the second kind is their laying down general rules which are conceived as more or less permanent. Such orders, each of which is at first quite independent and revocable at any moment, after the ground they cover has reached a certain extent, constitute a connected body of formulated law upon matters of procedure. As we have already seen, from the beginning of the 17th century the House of Commons has shown considerable activity iu this kind of autonomous legislation. In the course of time the constant repetition of certain well-tried orders, as opposed to special, temporary regulations, has led to the recognition of standing orders as a separate class of rules. Standing orders are regulations which have been expressly declared to be intended to hind all future parliaments, although the right is reserved of repealing them at any future time by a simple decision of the House.
In addition to the standing orders of a second category of procedure rules known as sessional orders has grown up.
I wish to repeat that sentence, and when I do so every member will see that it settles the whole point in controversy.
In addition to the standing orders a second category of procedure rules known as sessional orders has grown up.
So how aie sessional orders to be anything else than procedure rules?
These comprise regulations which the House expressly renews at the beginning of each session, making the principles contained in them binding for the duration of its currency. The number of sessional orders has never been large, and several of them by constant repetition, session after session, have practically become standing orders. There are also a number of rules not belonging to either of the foregoing classes, never expressly endowed with either short or long duration, which by virtue of continuous practice, have acquired the force of customary law. For more than Mr. MEIGHEN.
50 years it has been usual for the procedure, regulations and forms of all three kinds to be collected from time to time in a hand-hook under the editorship of the Clerk of the House for the time being; it is laid by the Speaker on the table of the House, and may, therefore, be regarded as an official statement.
So that' these three classes of procedure rules, standing orders, sessional orders and the other class of orders, constitute themselves with nothing else the procedure rules of the House of Commons of England. One class is just as much a portion of the procedure rules as another. They are all embodied in what is known as the official statement binding on the House of Commons of England. Now, I ask the hon. members of this House, by what authority we can dismember that official statement and say that one class only is a procedure rule and the other is not? By what authority can we tear limb from limb what is expressly laid down as the basis, and the comprehensive precise basis of. the procedure rules of the House of Commons of England? It is a matter of some importance that we get the whole benefit of our rules; that we be not robbed at any time of the real benefit of the rules of our House. If it is to be laid down that sessional orders are not included in the word 'rules' it may be a more serious matter for this House than perhaps we would at first anticipate. By the simple means of passing rule I of the rules_ of this House the Commons of Canada gained by one stroke the whole advantage _ of centuries of experience of the British House of Commons. They acquired the advantage of all the rules that that House had got together throughout centuries of the hardest experience, just such experience as we otherwise would have had to undergo. It is therefore I conceive, of great importance that we should not lightly throw away the benefit of any of our rules, more particularly that salutary rule I of this House. Now, Sir, what would result if this House were to lose the benefit of rule I? What would be the result if this House for all time were to be guided by the rule that sessional orders were not rules of the British House. I would like any han. gentleman in this House to show me by what authority for nine years in the House of Commons strangers were kept out of this House at the instance of Mr. Speaker, if not by virtue of a sessional order of the House of Commons of England. I would like any hon. member to show me by what authority even up to the present day strangers can be kent from blocking the thoroughfares to this House if not by the authority of a sessional order of the House of Commons of England. I would like also any hon. gentleman to tell me by what, regulations we are governed in the printing of our Votes and Proceedings if we do not

have the benefit of sessional orders that were in force in England on the 1st of July, 1867. And the most distinct and the most apparent loss we suffer is in respect to the very dilemma that we are placed in as to which I -put the question to Mr. Speaker on December 1st last-the situation that by virtue of having lost sessional orders we find ourselves in the absurd position of being made to say for all time any hon. member may sit for one, for two or for twenty seats, throughout the whole period of a parliament in this country. I do not need to go any further. I only purpose making such remarks as I conceive to be absolutely necessary to make clear that we must reaffirm what I think was misconstrued in the course of the reasoning by which the decision of December 2nd was arrived at. I regret it was so arrived at but we are bound by it and I bow with respect to that decision. However, let us not be bound by the reasoning that led to it; let us not lose the benefit of the salutary position that this House has 'always enjoyed, let us reaffirm it to-day. I therefore beg to move seconded by Mr. Marshall:
That Mr. Speaker do not now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Supply, but that it be resolved-
That in the judgment of this House sessional orders of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland in force on the 1st day of July, 1867, are within the meaning of the words ' rules, usages, and forms of proceeding ' as contained in rule I of the rules of the House of Commons of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman refers to 'Hansard' I think he will find that my statement is absolutely and literally correct,, but whether or no that is the case is of little consequence. The matter was brought up in the manner I have described, and the hon. the Speaker took time to consider his ruling in regard to it, and whatever may have been the form in which the question was presented for his consideration he considered it upon its merits and he pronounced his best judgment in regard to it. That judgment stands unquestioned; there was no challenge of it whatever. It was received in the silence and by the acquiescence of this House, and the House upon its being pronounced proceeded at once to other business. Now, the question is renewed in the form of an amendment to the motion to go into supply, and it is so renewed notwithstanding that upon the Order Paper there is a government notice of a motion for a committee to examine carefully the rules of the House and to report what changes in their opinion might be adopted with a view to simplify, accelerate and expedite its business, and notwithstanding the fact also that legislation to deal with this very subject has been introduced to this House and stands in the shape of Bill (No. 60) upon the Public Bills and Orders. And if any one wished to take exception to the course which has been pursued in making this motion to-day I venture to think, Mr. Speaker, that one so objecting would have been entitled to your ruling in his favour if he took the position that the course which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) has taken to-day was entirely out of order, because it deals solely and only with the subject matter of a Bill already upon the Order Paper and standing for consideration. But however irregular the course may be, which is taken to bring forward this question, the question might quite as well be dealt with now as at any time; and I venture to submit, Mr. Speaker, that the ruling you pronounced on this subject on the 2nd of December is in every respect correct and is one which ought to be supported and not overturned by the action of this House. The whole question is within a very narrow limit. I cannot pretend, and I do not want any one to suppose that I pretend, to think myself in the least degree a parliamentary authority, or to speak in the light of experience or of knowledge other than any one can have from reading our rules on the subject; and I want to speak of the matter solely and entirely in view of the language of that rule. I start from the position which I suppose is common ground that this is a case not expressly provided for in our parliamentary rules on the subject. Unless that common ground exists there is no room for

discussion at all. But assuming it to be a case not provided for in our existing rules, the question then narrows itself to whether or not the practice followed in England on the subiect is introduced into this country bv the first of our general rules, which provides for such cases as are not exnresslv mentioned here. That rule prescribes that in cases not provided for the rules, usages and forms of proceeding of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom which were in force on the first day of July, 1867, shall be followed/
Now, the first thing that any one would think of, it seems to me, in entering upon an inquiry upon this subject would be whether or not there was in force on the first of July, 1867, a rule of this character in England. You called attention, Sir, to that feature of the case in the considered ruling which you delivered on the 2nd of December inst. I understood the reference which you made in that ruling to the question whether or not the imperial parliament was then in session to be by way of illustrating the temporary character of the sessional orders which were under discussion by you. In some quarters I have seen during the last week criticisms of the ruling which you then pronounced upon the ground that is was based on that technical consideration. I certainly did not so understand it; and, reading it, I fail to see bow any one could think that the consideration of whether or not the sessional order in England was in force on the first of July, 1867, was in any degree the foundation of Mr. Speaker's decision in this House a week ago. But the fact that that inquiry necessarily falls to be made is of the utmost significance. It shows at once that the sessional order which is passed at the beginning of the session and which expires with the session is of temporary character, and is not at all on the same footing as a general parliamentary rule which endures from session to session and from parliament to parliament until it is revoked or varied. Our own rule calls attention in the most distinct manner to that very difference. In its opening statement that ' in all cases not provided for hereinafter or by sessional or other orders,' three different things are collated: provided for hereinafter is one; provided for by sessional orders is another: provided for bv other orders is a third. Those three different things are put in marked contra-distinction to the ' rules, usrgi s and forms of proceeding' which immediately afterwards are mentioned. The very wording of our general rule No. 1 points in the most distinct manner to the fact that there is some difference between a general rule, usage, or form of proceeding; and a sessional order. If one looks at Bourinot on the subject, one finds immediately what is the distinctive and Mr. AYLESWORTH.
essential character of a sessional order. At page 309, paragraph 4, he deals with sessional orders and resolutions, and he says, to read three sentences:
The House passes, in the course of every session, certain orders or resolutions, which are intended to have only a temporary effect on its proceedings, or to regulate the business of the' session. These orders generally relate to the times of adjournment, the arrangement of business, or the internal economy of the House, or to the presentation of certain papers in subsequent sessions. Up to the session of 1876, certain resolutions relative to the offer of money were formally proposed and agreed to at the commencement of every session, but when the rules were revised that year, these resolutions were placed among the permanent orders.
Does not every word of that mark the distinction between a mere sessional order, a temporary thing that may or may not apply to any subsequent session, and something which takes the place of a general rule or parliamentary practice which continues in force by reason of its own strength until it is either revoked, amended or in some way got rid of? The sessional order expires with the session. For instance, the resolution which from time to time we see passed as to the order of business on a Wednesday or on a Monday, as the session goes on towards its end; the resolution that the House shall have forenoon sessions or that it shall sit on Saturday-things of that sort are of an ephemeral character, I might almost say -are mere orders or resolutions for the doing of business in that particular session, and unless repeated have of course no force or effect in any subsequent session. And so, Mr. Speaker, I venture to think that your reference to the fact that it had not been made to appear to you whether or not the British House of Commons was in session on the first of July, 1867, was a very significant and pregnant reference. If the House was not in session on that day, the whole question falls to the ground without more ado There could not be any sessional order in force on that day, and there is no need to inquire further. If the House was in session on that day, the matter could not be quite disposed of on that ground, and accordingly you did not propose to dispose of it on that ground; but you faced the question squarely on the assumption that the House of Commons was in session' on the first of July, 1867, and you proceeded to inquire whether or not on that assumption a sessional order of the House of Commons which may have been passed for the session of 1867 could be held to have been introduced into this country by our rules.
Assuming then that a sessional order upon the subject of a member entitled to one or the other of two or more seats, being required within any limit of time to select which of those seats he would

hold-assuming that a sessional order upon that subject was passed by the British House of Commons in the session of 1867, and that the British House of Commons was in fact in session upon the 1st of July, 1867, the question is simply whether or not, under the language of our general rule, such a sessional, temporary, evanescent order was introduced into the practice of this parliament. What is the language of rule 1? According to it, the things which were introduced into the present practice of this parliament are not the sessional orders, but the rules, usages and forms of proceeding of the English House of Commons as they stood on the 1st of July, 1867. Under which one of these three heads' does a sessional order fall? Is it a rule, a usage or a form of proceeding? I confess that I awaited with considerable interest the discussion of this matter by the hon. gentleman, to know under which of those three heads he would contend a sessional order was included. He could scarcely argue that it was a mere form of proceeding. The term ' form of proceeding ' surely means something entirely different. I had thought that possibly his argument would have been that it was included under the word ' usage'. That word i3, perhaps, of somewhat elastic meaning, but I should suppose it includes something which was not put into any form of words, some such thing as the ancient traditional usage or custom which every member of the House of Commons in this country or in England exercises, if he pleases, to sit in his seat with his hat on notwithstanding that the House is in session	and the
Sneaker in the chair, or the usage which exists in England, but not here, of taking a particular point of order seated and with the hat on. Usages of that kind, which Test on custom or tradition, cannot be described in any set form of words. It is not urged, however, that this question is governed by the introduction into this parliament of the usages of the British parliament, but the argument is that it falls under the phrase rules of the English House of Commons. But take the language of our rule 1 itself, and you will find the clearest and most distinct line of opposition and contrast drawn between the rules which are introduced and the sessional or other orders which are mentioned in the line before as things which govern cases not provided for expressly. The contrast is marked. The nature, the substance of the thing itself demonstrates that a sessional order is, as Bourinot points out, something very different from a permanent rule of the House which does not expire at prorogation but continues from session to session and from parliament to parliament. I certainly could not, in such light as I have on the subject, come to the con-42
elusion that your ruling, Mr. Speaker, given a week ago, was erroneous.

speechtext:
I wish to say with regard to this question that so eminent an authority on parliamentary procedure as Redlich says, in Vol. 2, page 6, referring to rules of parliamentary procedure:
In addition to the standing orders, a second category of procedure rules, known as sessional orders, has grown up.
Can there be any doubt, in view of this high authority, that a sessional order is a parliamentary rule? The ordinary rules of the House and sessional orders are all rules of parliamentary procedure according to this eminent authority.
These comprise regulations which the House expressly renews at the beginning of each session, making the principles contained in them binding for the duration of its currency. The number of sessional orders has never been large, and several of them, by constant repetition, session after session, have practically become standing orders.
In a foot note which indicate those referred to are the following:
(1) Double election returns; (2) exclusion of peers from voting; (3) prohibition against interference of peers in elections; (4) bribery at elections; (5) tampering with witnesses; (6) false evidence given to the House or one of its committees; (7) direction to the police to keep the passages to the House clear; (8) regulations as to printing the votes and proceedings; (9) regulations as to printing the journal.
I wish to point out that if rule 1 of our orders were not so construed as to include the sessional and standing orders, this House has no authority to patrol and police its corridors. The only authority for our doing this is the sessional orders whicli were in force in England on the 1st day of July, 1867. We have followed those orders with regard to other matters heretofore, and it was only within recent years that we made rules regarding the printing of the Votes and Proceedings and regulations regarding the printing of the Journals. And it was only in recent years that we passed an Act dealing with false evidence given the House or one of its committees. Up to that time we had absolutely no authority in those matters except the sessional and standing orders in force in the British House of Commons on the 1st of July, 1867, and I submit, with all due deference to so eminent an authority as the Minister of Justice, that the sessional and standing orders enforced in England on the 1st of July, 1867, are rules to which this House, under rule 1, is subject.

I have very little to add to what has been said on this subject. The argument of my hon. friend the



Minister of Justice amounts simply to this, that in determining whether or not a rule of the British House of Commons is a rule within the meaning of the statute and of our standing orders, you must look, not to the language of the rule, but to the probable length of its duration. That is the test fixed by my hon. friend. The Minister of Justice contends .that it is not the character of the order that determines whether or not it is a rule, but the question whether or not it shall remain in force one, two or three sessions, or indefinitely. I need not appeal to lawyers,
T appeal to every layman ,as to whether that is common sense. Every one will realize that it is not. Neither, in my humble opinion, is it common law. Why, every one of the rules, every _ one of the standing orders of the imperial House or our House, with very few exceptions, might be put into the form of sessional orders and the business of that House carried on exactly as it is to-day. Yet the Minister of Justice, in that case, would stand in this House and seriously declare that the British House of Commons had no rules-for that would be the direct result of the argument he has addressed or the House this afternoon. I would like to ask the Minister of Justice this: If these sessional orders, so-called, were limited in their duration, not by one session but by three, four or five sessions, would he still contend that they were not Tules? I must confess that I am unable to apprehend the argument of the hon. gentleman. To say that the character of a rule is to be determined, not by its nature, but by the limit of its duration-well, if I might be permitted to use a common expression, I would say that that was the limit itself.
Mr. Speaker, does the Minister of Justice realize that some of the most important legislation in Great Britain to-day, the most vital, that in connection with the allimportant subject of the defence of the empire, is passed every session? And if any man asks him what the law of Great Brittain. is, for example, with regard to mutiny, would he tell that man that Great Britain has no law at all on that subject, because the Mutiny Act is limited in its duration and is passed every year? Yet that was exactly the argument of the hon. minister this afternoon. The Minister of Justice says that in his opinion the subject is not open to argument. I agree with him entirely, but in a sense absolutely the contrary of that which he had in mind.

I have been a good many years in parliament, and I have realized by long experience that the law of parliament is far more difficult and far more intricate than my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) and my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie
(Mr. Meighen) seem to think. The law of parliament is full of difficulty; it is a maze in which it is very easy to lose one s way. Parliamentary authorities vary very much in their interpretation of the rules. It is a matter of notoriety that, in England, the best minds in parliament, the most eminent men who have ever sat there, have been found arguing on one side and on the other of questions that have arisen in connection with these matters. The whole law of parliament is, in its origin, the arbitrary regulations of the House of Commons-[DOT] and I use that word ' arbitrary ' in no offensive sense, rules which have been established from time to time. Some of these rules are temporary in their nature, while some are permanent. I confess that it is difficult not to realize that there is a distinction between a temporary and a permanent rule. The very names are different-some are called rules and others are called by other names, as usages, sessional orders, and so on. I apprehend that the average member of the House will have some difficulty in coming to the conclusion that Mr. Speaker, who gave to this question the best judgment he could bring to bear upon it, was wrong. But it would be difficult for the average member to say that the Minister of Justice, an authority in law. was wrong. And I may say that it would be difficult for any one to say that the hon. leader of the opposition, in his view of the matter, is wrong-he is a good lawyer. All this only shows the difficulty of coming to a conclusion on such a question. When this matter was brought to his attention, Mr. Speaker gave to it his best consideration and judgment. He reviewed the facts and authorities and came to the conclusion that there was no such rule of the House as was contended for by my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie. I dare say it is difficult to say who was right and who was wrong. The ruling of Mr. Speaker may be right or it may be wrong. In fact, Mr. Speaker himself did not pretend to say finally that he was right, but intimated that the subject was full of difficulties and suggested what he thought would be the proper course for the House to follow. Let me call the attention of the House again to the ruling of Mr. Speaker:
My ruling is, therefore, that there is nothing in the rule of this House requiring a member who has been returned for more than one constituency to elect within any prescribed time for which of such constituencies he will sit. But, in my opinion, it is eminently desirable that some definite rule and practice on the subject should he established.
And he went on to say:
The House has a Standing Committee for the purpose of considering such questions- the Committee on Privileges and Elections- and I will suggest that at an early date the

Who is the member, on that side or on this, who will undertake to say that the argument of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice was wrong, or will undertake to say that the argument of the leader of the opposition was wrong, or that the ruling of Mr. Speaker was wrong? I think that every member will have no hesitation in saying that he would rather not take it upon himself to assert that Mr. Speaker was wrong in his ruling, and that the rule spoken of by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie was actually in existence. speechtext:
The question now before the House is certainly a most interesting one from at least two standpoints. If we consider for the moment the party, politically speaking, who have proposed the question, and the party, politically speaking, who oppose the question, we must surely think that the party in power have travelled a tremendously long distance since they prided themselves on being ' democrats to the hilt.' One would hardly believe it possible, even in this western hemisphere, with all the enterprise and progress that we claim, that the Reform party would, be the party found questioning the right of the people to secure representation in parliament. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) has referred to some matters on which we might agree. I suppose it will be admitted that we can agree on this, that no member sits in this House as the representative of Ottawa, or as the representative of Quebec, or any other locality, but that under our parliamentary system, inasmuch as all the people cannot assemble within the halls of parliament, the country is divided into certain districts, each one of which sends a representative to Ottawa to represent, not that district, but the whole people of Canada. Therefore, if this be true-and I hesi-421
tate not to say will not be questioned as a matter of law-it follows that every person in Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, is deprived of his proper representation in this House when, although the law says that there shall be 221 representatives, the Prime Minister says there shall be only 220. Now, we come to consider this case thoroughly understanding that, from some cause or other, _ the people of this country are being deprived of one representative, and as it has not been alleged, even by the Prime Minister, that the rights depend not on a member holding two seats as against his holding three or more, then the principle which is being contended for by the Minister of Justice and the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is that, if the government in power were able to carry all the seats in the country by running a few men to hold a number of seats each, they might sit here as a House of Commons although they might be only a half or a quarter the number provided by the law, and they might sit for a full term of five years and the people would have no remedy or redress-nay, Sir. they would not even have ground of complaint concerning what some would think an outrage on their rights.
It would be bad enough in all conscience if the old Tory party had been thus endeavouring to trample on the rights of the people, but for the Reform party, a Reform party of the most progressive continent and the most progressive country in that continent, to endeavour thus to trample on the rights of the people, is indeed somewhat remarkable. I was pleased to see that the right hon. gentleman who leads this House did not himself endeavour to support the argument of the Minister of Justice. The right hon. gentleman, although he is occupying these seats during the whole of last session and so far this session, has no other justification than to put a motion on the Order Paper appointing a committee of the most eminent men selected from both sides of the House, to revise the rules, and the implication comes in that in terms surely there must be something wrong in the rules. Now, if everything was right and proper, if everything was satisfactory, why should these need to revise the rules? Do they intend to improve them on the ground that they are not quite right and proper? But if one is to understand the right hon. gentleman, as I think he may fairly be understood, his whole remarks were to this effect: A lamentable state of affairs existed, and I am in possession of -I won't say stolen goods-but if any hon. gentleman can suggest any way within a reasonable time, without any inconvenience, by which I can get rid of part of the goods, I am prepared to bow to their decision. Now when we look at this matter

as a question in which the government party is depriving a part of the people of their proper representation, I think we may go a step further and see on what grounds they claim so to deprive the people. When this matter first came before the House and the point was raised the Speaker, after first reading the rule, said:
In the imperial parliament the matter under consideration is dealt with by sessional orders which are renewed by the House of Commons from session to session, and which expire at prorogation.
Now here is the point:
The sessional order on the subject which was, presumably, passed by the Imperial House in 1867 may or may not have been in force on the 1st day of July in that year, depending on whether the House was then in session or had been prorogued before that date.
There is no doubt in the world, nobody will dispute, that if the imperial House was not in force on the 1st of July, 1867, then this rule would not apply, and could not be invoked. But one would have thought that the Minister _ of Justice, in referring to this matter, might have given the case sufficient attention to find out whether the imperial House was in session at that date. Surely it is not a difficult matter to visit the library, which is near at hand, where he could have found volumes to show whether it was in session or not. He could have found the ' Hansards' of the imperial House of that date, and the Journals of the House, which would have supplied him with the necessary information. So, unless we are deceived by the books placed in our hands in the parliamentary library, the imperial House was in session on that date; and if it was, why lose so much time in discussing this simple question? Then, Sir, the next point the Minister of Justice makes, in reading this rule, is that the sessional orders are different from all other orders. Of course they are different; a pink apple is different from a green apple and yet one may be just as much an apple as the other. A sessional order is different' from a permanent order, and I sincerely trust the Minister of Justice was enlightening his own side of the House, and not pretending that he was enlightening the members on this side of the House. But the point is not whether there is a difference between a sessional order and a permanent order, but the point is, when you come to read the rule, what is the meaning of certain words in that rule? If we can agree on what is meant by one of our own rules, then we need not bother about the difference between a sessional order and a permanent order. No one will differ from me in this reading of the rule. Now I propose to read the rule, eliminating the various words that have no reference at all to the question Mr. NORTHRUP.
before us, and I fancy that no one will say that I am not reading the rule fairly, it being understood that I am eliminating no material words:
In all cases not provided for hereinafter by sessional orders, the rules of proceeding-
Now what is the meaning of the phrase 'rules of proceeding'? Because if provision is made by sessional orders, and if we are dealing with rules of proceeding, then the argument of the Minister of Justice falls to the ground. Now what is the meaning of the words 'rules of proceeding'? It is true that this clause reads:	The
rules, usages and forms of proceeding*. But I imagine nobody will dispute the grammatical meaning of the words as I read them at first. Now when we come to find out the meaning of the words 'rules of proceeding', let us look at Redlich, than whom no higher authority, exists. We are trying to find out the meaning of the words 'rules of proceeding'. Redlich says:
In addition to the standing orders, a second category of procedure rules known as sessional orders, has grown up.
Now we go a step further. We have on the one hand the Minister of Justice trying to interpret the rules of proceeding, * and on the other hand we have the procedure rules. He did not pretend to distinguish between rules of proceeding and procedure rules; and if they meant one and the same thing, as surely they do, then Redlich will say that procedure rules are known as sessional orders, and if procedure rules are known as sessional orders, it cannot be monstrously absurd to call sessional orders procedure rules. And if procedure rules mean the same as rules of proceeding, then they comply with the very words of the rule we are discussing as one of the rules and orders of this House. Now look at another authority, May, perhaps no better authority couid be found, and I read on page 148:
At the commencement of each session both Houses agree to orders and resolutions, which are renewed from year to year.
The operation of orders or resolutions of either House of which the duration is undetermined, is not settled upon any certain principle. By the custom of parliament they would he concluded by a prorogation: but many of them are, as part of the settled practice of parliament, observed in succeeding sessions, and by different parliaments, without any formal renewal or repetition.
So, Sir, wa find that not only are sessional orders within the meaning of the rule particularly, but we find that sessional orders are in many cases observed as being part of the settled practice of parliament, and observed in succeeding sessions and by different parliaments, and without any formal renewal or repetition. Now when we get that far we begin to find

that the difference between sessional orders and other orders mav not by any means be the same as the Minister of Justice imagines. And I am sure, Sir, the members on this side of the House, if they cannot agree with all the Minister of Justice has said, at least will be quite ready to agree with his introductory remark that he did not pretend to have any familiarity with constitutional law or the procedure of houses of parliament.
In this same work, May, at page 148, is an illustration of what I have just read, of sessional orders becoming practically permanent orders and being held to be binding, not only in successive sessions, but in successive parliaments without any re-enactment. Some 15 or 20 examples of this occurring in England are given. Take, for example, the rule that the Speaker cannot take the chair if 40 members are not present. That rule came into existence on the 6th of January, 1640, and was the law in England up to the date of the publication of this 11th edition of May's Parliamentary Practice, in the year 1906. I shall not take up the time of the House in reading other examples. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie has shown this House that under English procedure the right hon. gentleman who leads this House is wrongfully depriving the people of Canada of one of the seats to which thev are entitled. I know that some of the representatives of the smaller provinces would not consider it a grievance if the seat which to him is so contemptibly insignificant should be given to one of these provinces. Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island would rejoice if the seat were allotted to them. I trust the right hon. gentleman will see that in setting such an example as this, a blow is being struck not merely at the parliamentary reputation of. the people, not merely at the rights of the people, but at the position, at the dignity of this House. We hear it said continually that our courts and judges are entitled to the most profound respect, and a man either in this House or elsewhere will always feel a tremendous sense of responsibility in attacking our judiciary; but the same men who speak in this way of our judges will sav that the highest court in the land is the court of parliament. If one of our judges should go wrong-and it is the proud boast of Canada that we have never yet had the necessity of impeaching a judge-it would be considered a national disgrace by every Canadian. Then what are we to think if in the highest court of Canada, composed of those who make the laws for others who thus observe them, we find that by the right hon. gentleman who by such an overwhelming majority leads and governs that House, the law of the land is broken.

speechtext: I am not asking for any amendment to the rules of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: But, my hon. friend is seeking to put an interpretation upon a rule of the House, and whether he is right or wrong in his view, it should first have full and mature consideration by a committee of this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext:
Is the hon. minister aware that the most important change ever made in the rules of the British

House of Commons was made without any reference whatever to a committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: To what does the hon. gentleman refer?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: I am referring to the first closure resolutions which were moved in the House -by Mr. Gladstone and which were not referred to a committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is right in that respect. It was passed by the House almost unanimously and without any great debate; but he must admit that the procedure we have followed in this House, when we have made or amended any of our rules, has been to refer those rules to a committee to be fully considered.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: I am not criticising that practice at all. I was simply saying that it was something departed from, and I did not consider this to be a proposal to amend the rule.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: It amounts to the same thing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: Allow me to make myself clear. Suppose, for example, that there had been an inadvertent decision denying the right of a man to move an amendment on going into Supply, and on the day alter some hon. member should declare that according to the rules and usages of the British House of Commons or of this House no hon. member has the right to move an amendment to Supply. This is precisely of the same nature.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext:
I cannot admit that. The interpretation which my hon. friend wants to put upon the first of our rules is a most important one, and before the House passes judgment upon it, I think it should be fully considered by a committee of this House or by the full House in committee. That has been our procedure in the past. Let us consider for a moment what the declaration is which we are called upon to make:
That in the judgment of this House the sessional orders of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland in force on the first day of July, 1867, are within the meaning of the words, ' rules, usages and forms of proceeding/ as contained in rule 1 of the rules of the House of Commons of Canada.
I say this is a most serious declaration. What are we asked to embody in it? We are asked to embody rules which for forty years this parliament has not been supposed to put in force. I think, before we incorporate in our rules the important declaration made in this motion, we should inquire a little to find out how far we would be going by such a declaration. My hon. friend may be right in his interpretation of the law; but at the same time is it
advisable to adopt a sweeping declaration of that kind without having a committee of this House to investigate fully how far it would carry us? I may say that I do not think the procedure which my hon. friend is following is the proper procedure, and for this reason. My hon. friend knows that when a decision has been rendered by the Speaker, that decision stands as final unless there is an appeal from it. Rule 18 says:
The Speaker may permit debate of the point of order before rendering his decision, but such debate must be strictly relevant to the point of order taken. The Speaker shall decide upon the point of order, which decision shall be subject to appeal to the House, but without debate. If there be no appeal, the decision of the Chair shall be final. ,
If I remember rightly, my hon. friend himself raised the question the other day, and appealed to the Speaker for a decision.
A. decision was rendered by the Speaker, and that was final unless an appeal was taken from it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: What was the point of order Mr. Speaker decided?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: I understand that my hon. friend brought before Mr. Speaker the point that a member of this House had no right to sit for two seats-that he had to make a declaration within a certain period, according to the rule that was in existence in the House of Commons of England in 1867.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think that was a point of order within the meaning of the rule?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: My hon. friend called the Speaker's attention to that, and the Speaker decided that that rule was not in force; and I say that when the Speaker puts an interpretation upon a rule of this House and there is no appeal to the House from his decision, that becomes the judgment of the House. In this case my hon. friend is asking us to make a most important declaration, embodying in our rules all the sessional orders of the parliament of the United Kingdom that were in force on the first of July, 1867.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: It is not even that. It is only those which deal with matters not expresssly provided for in our own rules.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext:
Of course our rules are not very extensive, they are not nearly as extensive as those existing in England. At all events, my hon. friend is asking us to declare that all the rules and sessional orders passed by the parliament of the United Kingdom from 1801 to 1867 should form part of our rules of procedure. This is a most important declaration; we do not know where it would land us: and before

deciding such a question, I think it should be referred to a committee of the House to investigate how far it would take us.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: Will the minister say whether standing orders are within the meaning of the rule?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: Yes, I think so.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: Does not his argument apply equally to those, and would not a committee of this House be equally necessary to decide what a standing order would lead to?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: I must say to my hon. friend that I have not given that question very much consideration. I do not claim to know everything about that. While I have given some study to the rules of the House, I must admit that I do not know them all and am liable to make mistakes. At the same time I would not be prepared to declare offhand whether a sessional order did or did not form part of the rules of this House. I should make considerable distinction between standing orders and sessional orders. My own opinion is that although the standing rules of the British House of Commons form part of our rules, their sessional orders must not be applied in the same way. Possibly after studying the matter more carefully, I may come to a different conclusion; but for the time being I am strongly of the opinion that the sessional orders of the British House of Commons in force on the 1st of July, 1867, do not form a part of our standing orders.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: Has the hon. minister any authority which says that a sessional order is not a rule?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext: I say that the sessional orders of the British House of Commons should not be considered as part of our rule No. 1, because what is there contemplated is, not the rules which were in existence in England one, two or three sessions, but the standing rules which had been in existence for years and which were considered almost as important as the privileges themselves. That is the construction I would put upon rule No. 1. When my hon. friend asks us to declare that all the sessional orders of the British House of Commons form part of our rules, he is embarking on very dangerous ground and may find himself, after giving the matter more consideration, entirely _ mistaken. He may find that such a decision would incorporate in our procedure, rules which parliament never intended to form part of our standing rules. That is my view and I am sure the hon. gentleman will be well advised, under the circumstances, not to press his motion.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext:
If I understand rightly the argument of the hon. gentlemen op-
Mr. BRODEUR
posite, they contend that there is no law, order or precedents in this country requiring a man who has been elected for more than one constituency to resign one of these seats at any time during the parliament for which he was elected, 'that in itself would strike the people, it seems to me, as a very startling proposition. It simply amounts to this, that a man might be returned for two or three or ten constituencies and sit for them all during a whole parliament, and that there is no law, constitution, order or rule requiring him to resign all but the one seat. I have here Bourinot's parliamentary procedure, a work which is accepted generally as indisputable authority in matters of this kind. Just listen for one moment to what he says on page 245:
In case a member is returned for two constituencies, lie must make his election for which of the places he will serve by formally resigning his seat when the House is in session. This election may be made by a member from his place in the House or in the usual legal communication to the Speaker.
If that authority be good (and as such it is quoted by you, Mr. Speaker, almost daily), the contention of hon. gentlemen opposite is erroneous, and by inference the sessional order of the British House of Commons, in force on the 1st of July, 1867, are included in the words 'rules, usages and forms of procedure' mentioned in rule 1. Otherwise there is no ground for Bourinot's statement that a member elected for several constituencies must select one and resign the others. If the sessional orders of the .British House of Commons, as they existed on the 1st of July, 1867, do not govern this case and are not included in our rule No. 1, then Bourinot had no ground for making the statement I have just read.
Further in section 1 of chapter 41 of the Statutes of Canada, 1907, it is provided that the House of Commons shall consist of 221 members. But if one member may represent two seats, then the House does not consist of 221 members but only of 220, and the right hon. gentleman who should be the last man to violate the constitution, has been representing two seats in this House in defiance of section 1 of chapter 41 Statutes of Canada, 1907.
There is a provision that where a member's seat is contested, he cannot resign until the suit is disposed of. But the protest against the right hon. gentleman for one of the seats in Ottawa was disposed of in June last. It is perfectly clear what the duty of the right hon. gentleman then was. Can there be any doubt about it? Is there any layman or lawyer who would not say that it was the duty of the right hon. gentleman, when that case was

disposed of, to elect whether he should sit for one of the seats in Ottawa or for Quebec East, for both of which he had been elected. So that since the month of June last the right hon. the Prime Minister has been violating the constitution of this country. This House should by law con-' sist of 221 members, but we are short of that number because the right hon. gentleman is occupying two seats, and all this trouble has arisen simply because he has failed to do his duty, in fact we seem to have reached the stage when no right of the people in this country is too sacred to be sacrificed to the necessities of political exigencies by the party now in power.
I submit that there is no getting away from the statement I started out with, if Bourinot is right in saying that a man elected for more than one seat must select one and resign from the other, then the sessional orders in force in England on the 1st of July, 1867, must be applicable here.
