speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: ['Monday, December 13, 1909.']

I see in the Auditor General's Report at page J-18 an item of $1,448.66 paid to 14 special officers of this department. I assume that these men were paid about $100 per annum each for special services at Windsor, Ontario. I would like to ask the minister what duties these men performed, at whose recommendation they were appointed, and what special qualifications they have for such duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is the expenditure under this vote. These officers are our regular supervising excise officers, who are assigned to special services largely or altogether in connection with distilleries. Their duties are very exacting, very important and their hours very long. Each officer in charge of a distillery has to be on duty from seven o'clock in the morning until six o'clock in the evening. Their long hours and their responsible duties entitle them to some consideration over and above their regular salaries, which are fixed by the Civil Service Act, and therefore for these extra services they ^re paid the duty pay which has been paid by the department for 35 years. It is because this work is increasing somewhat that we are asking for $2,000 more this year than we asked for last year.
On whose recommendation are these officers appointed, do they undergo any examination, and have they any special qualifications for this kind of work?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
All the officers of mv department have to undergo the Civil Service examination before they can be appointed permanently. If an officer is put in temporarily, it is only with the understanding that he will pass the examination
at the first available opportunity. All these excise officers who are in charge of distilleries and receive this extra duty pay have passed up from one grade to another and have passed the examination for promotion required by the department. They are nearly all very old officials.

I would like to know whether the doctrine laid down by the Finance Minister so clearly the' other evening is applied to my hon. friend's department, and whether these are political rewards to these men. The Finance Minister stated that the policy of the government was to give offices to their own political supporters.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not exactly. What I said was that if they did, I did not see why my hon. friend should complain.

I accept the explanation, but what I want to know is whether, in the appointment of officers of this kind, my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue, applies the policy laid down by the Finance Minister, namely, that where an office is vacant and he can find a supporter of the government to fill it, it will go to him in preference to a Conservative, no matter what may be the qualifications of the latter.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The Department of Inland Revenue does not follow the practise my hon. friend has mentioned, that is, if a vacancy occurs in the position of a first or second-class excise officer, a new man will not be put directly in that position. In the Inland Revenue Department that would be impossible. Our special class officers, our first or second-class officers, are all men who have risen from the ranks after long service and who have passed, not only the original entrance examination, but the promotion examinations as well. They must have a knowledge of the details and the workings of the office, and I cannot remember any new men having been appointed to such office under my tenure of that department. Take for instance in the case of distilleries, the officer must be competent to see that the revenue of the government is properly safe-guarded, and to do that he must have had some experience in a lower branch, so that new men are not put in these positions at all.
What about the new men appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: They are appointed to the lower grades at $500 a year an,d are very seldom given an appointment to a higher grade.

My hon. friend has answered many unasked questions, but he has failed to measure up the question I put to him. What I want to know is whether, when my hon. friend makes an appoint-

ment in his department, whether it be to a minor or a more important grade, he follows the policy laid down by the Finance Minister, that to the victor belong the spoils or, in other words, that these new men must be supporters of the party.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: As regards the appointment of new officials, we accept men who are qualified to fill these lower vacancies, and other things being equal we give the preference, of course, to our political friends. The appointments are very few indeed, and those are to the lower grades, and the offices in such grades are hardly worthy of acceptance, as $500 per year is not a great inducement to outsiders to take them. We do not put new appointees over the heads of officers in the department, but where a man is recommended to me by a political friend, and we have the assurance that he is competent, we most unquestionably give him the preference.
How are the recommendations made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Personally, verbally, in writing and in many ways toy members of parliament and others. There is_ no particular system, but I generally satisfy myself that the applicant is fit for the position. I have very frequently indeed sent the name of the party recommended to the collector of Inland Revenue in that particular district and asked him to advise me confidentially if the applicant is fit to be appointed to the service.

That is very frank, and I wish to compliment the Minister of Finance upon his influence in the cabinet. That influence seems to reach out to all these departments. His colleague has been very frank in admitting that these new appointments he has mentioned are given to party supporters and that no Conservative need apply. That is the policy of the government clearly announced. I was afraid there might be some disagreement in the cabinet, but all the ministers seem to think alike on that subject, and the country will understand that this government, which came into office with so many professions of a higher standard of politics, has reached the point that no new appointments can be made to his department except to a government supporter.
understood by our friends across the border where they mean a great deal more than the meaning I would give them. The question to determine is, first, what these spoils are. I would not consider that an office already held by a respectable Conservative was a spoils that must be got rid of. But if a vacancy occurred in the public service and there was a good Liberal capable of filling the place, and if we passed him over and gave the place to one of my hon. friend's friends, then we ought to be turned out.
Duty pay to officers serving longer hours at other than special survey, $1,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This is on the line of the last vote. It is to enable the department to pay duty pay to deserving officers engaged at other than special survey on account of their long hours and attendance, and in some cases the character of their work. These officers serve from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m., and this vote is paid to officers in the bonded manufactories.

This service is a technical service to a large extent. Have any men been appointed to this service since the minister took office who have not passed the Civil Service examination, and if so, how many?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: There have been appointments made to deputy collector-ships where the appointees have not passed the examination, the law not requiring that they should. All temporary appointees are expected to pass an examination, and they are not put on permanently and do not receive the annual increment of five per cent of salary until they do pass. It is quite true that in the outside service quite a num ber of men in the lower ranks have not yet passed the examination. Almost every time an examination is held a large number of our officers go up and try; some pass, and some fail and try again; some of them probably will never pass the examination. Some of them are very good officers and trustworthy men. I think perhaps out of 300 or 400 officers, 50 or 60 have not passed the examination.
Does this item cover those men in the service supervising what is known as the blending of liquors?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has been here all these years, and if he has only made that discovery now, he is somewhat duller than I took him to be. The only exception I take to his remarks is where he attributed to me the phrase ' to tlie victor belongs the spoils.' I never used the words in that particular sense which he applies to them, and in which they are Mr. BLAIN.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This item has no reference to what my hon. friend mentions. It refers to duty pay to officers in charge of bonded manufacturing establishments, for the manufacture of vinegar for instance, where officials have to be present from early in the morning till late at night. It is responsible work, and this extra pay is for services rendered. It attaches to the

office rather than to the man, it is not a portion of his salary at all.

I have heard that repeated several times. But I want to ask the minister if he has not special officers in charge of the manufacture of blended liquors, and what are the regulations in his department in that respect?
. Mr. TEMPLEMAN. There is no such thing.
' A. CURRIE. What machinery has the minister got for enforcing the statute that covers the case of blending and the licensing of blenders?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I suppose my hon. friend is referring to the compounding of liquors?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is nearly the same thing. There are licenses issued to a number of firms to compound liquors. As my hon. friend knows, all this liquor is duty paid before they can compound it. The only interest the department has is to collect the revenue.
I understand they use liquor in vinegar factories.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is not compounded.

I am well aware it is not compounded, but it is used in some instances. A vinegar manufacturer can purchase his alcohol duty paid and manufacture vinegar from it. I suppose the department has seen fit to place officers in charge of these factories to see that that law is not violated.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
In a bonded manufacture such as a vinegar factory we have officers. They manufacture in bond. Of course, the alcohol is converted into vinegar, and our officers see that the revenue is safeguarded. But that is a different thing altogether from the compounding of alcohol. In that case the liquor is duty . paid beforehand, so that the revenue could not possibly be defrauded.
Mr. .T, A. CURRIE. I do not wish to delay the minister; but I understand that there is a great deal of fraud committed in connection with the blending of liquor under licenses issued by the department. I understand that blenders buy cheap alcohol, that they mix all kinds of material with it, and manufacture so-called corn liquors which they sell throughout the country. For instance, a large quantity of what they call Scotch whisky is sold in this country, which is really manufactured by these people; also Egremont Mint and Benedictine are sold as foreign liquors, though they are manufactured by our Canadian vendors out of alcohol and other specific mixtures. They have brands upon them of firms supposed to be located in France, and Portugal, and in Scotland. Now that really constitutes a fraud on the public, a greater fraud even than the sale of unlicensed liquor. If a manufacturer wishes to put up Canadian whisky in bottles, he must place a seal on it, and of course that is done in bond. But have any steps been taken by the department to look into this matter, and have any representations been made to them on that question? We see reports in the newspapers of men dying from the effects of partaking of liquor which contains chloral hydrate and other drugs. No doubt the hon. minister saw the item in the papers with regard to Fort William and the northwest section of Ontario generally. Does not the minister think that some steps should be taken to meet cases of this kind, prevent adulteration and put a stop to the fraudulent marking of liquors with the names of manufacturers, or alleged manufacturers, in other countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: 1 am inclined to think that the fraudulent marking of alcoholic beverages would come under the Criminal Code. It has nothing to do with the Department of Inland Revenue.

If a man were to put on goods manufactured in Canada the label of, let us say, Lea and Perrin, I sup-oose that would be a fraud. But if he were to put on the name of some suppositious manufacturer in Glasgow or Birmingham, would that be a fraud?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It would not be an offence against the Inland Revenue Act, but it might be against the Criminal Code. I am not familiar enough with the penalties under the Criminal Code in relation to false markings to say whether misrepresentation of that kind would be counted a fraud or not, but I assume it would be. With regard to the purity of whisky, it is a fact that during last summer the Department of Inland Revenue made large collections of liquors as sold over the bar in many places in Ontario and even in Manitoba where statements were made that impure or poisonous stuff was sold over the bar. Analyses were made, and in almost every instance the report of our chemist was that nothing of a deleterious nature -nothing more deleterious than the whisky itself; nothing of a poisonous character -was added. Rarely anything more than alcohol or water was found to have been contained in any of the samples. For myself, I have very grave doubts about these reports concerning poisonous liquors

being sold. I read the despatch in -the newspapers relating to what happened at Fort William or Port Arthur. The offence of adulteration there referred to does not come under the Inland Revenue law. It may be possible that some foolish saloon man, thinking he could make cheap beverages, would try to doctor it up with noxious drugs. But we cannot be held responsible for that. The offence would he punishable no doubt, under the Criminal Code. The purity of liquor, if it is ever going to be dealt with, I suppose will have to be determined by standard to be decided upon by the officers of the Inland Revenue Department in connection with the standards for foods, upon which, as a matter of fact, the department is at present engaged.

I have looked over the returns published by the department in connection with this collection of liquors to which the minister has referred, and I notice that there is an absence of deleterious products ; but I notice also that there is a pretty constant addition of twenty-five per cent of water to the liquor sold throughout the country. Does not it occur to the minister that it would be wise, in the interest of his department and for the increase of the revenue, if some method were devised by which the sellers of liquors of that description could be punished? It would appear that it is possible to secure twenty-five per cent more revenue which now the hotelkeeper and middle-man are taking.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The department cannot he defrauded in that way. Our_excise duty is based on the measured proof gallon, and this must be paid when it leaves the bonding warehouse after being purchased by private parties, of course they can put in what they like. They may sell it at proof, or at fifty per cent under proof-just as weak as they can deceive the public into taking. But there is something in the point that the hon. member (Mr. Currie) makes. I suppose there should be a standard of strength for whisky. If we establish a standard providing that there should be so much alcohol and so much water, then if there be more water, that would be a violation of the law and punishable as such. The question is, what can we do? The temperance men will say that the lower you put the standard the better-the more water there is in the whisky the less harm it will do. But we are grappling with the question of fixing a standard for foodstuffs of all kinds and for drinks, including alcoholic drinks, and we hope, before many weeks, to be able to submit a set of standards under which the Adulteration of Foods Act may be better enforced. That is, of course, an enlargement of the subject actually under discussion. But I hope to fix standards for foodstuffs and liquors.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: I do not wish to delay the committee, but I would like to ask another question. There is an impression abroad in this country that the Scotch whisky sold here is the product of the old pot still. It is sent into this country by Scotch distillers and sold as Scotch whisky. Now, the minister is aware that there has been considerable agitation and, in fact, litigation, in the old country over the question of what constitutes Scotch whisky. But it has been shown, apart altogether from the question of whether all Scotch whisky is the product of the pot still or of the fractional still, that there is such a thing as real Scotch whisky which is the product of the Scotch still which was known before the fractional or silent still was brought into use. All the whisky made in Canada is the product of the silent still, and the distilleries here are required to mature their product, I understand, for three years before it is sold to the public. But here is where the trouble comes in: A distiller in Scotland or England who manufactures with the silent still turns out exactly the same product as our own distillers, and, by simply reducing the strength of that spirit, putting in some flavouring matter, to give it the flavour of Scotch whisky-such as wine or a touch of pyro-gallic acid to give it a smoky smell and taste-he is allowed to ship that stuff into Canada and sell it in this country within thirty days of the time it leaves the still. Whilst the very same product manufactured in Canada by the very same process, without the addition of these flavouring extracts, is required to be held in bond three years. Would it not be fair that some steps should be taken by the Excise Department to stop the importation of any hard spirits such as whiskies which have not been matured for the same length of time in bond in this country as Canadian made spirits are matured? This liquor is manufactured abroad, by men who run these silent stills, from refuse of all kinds, beet root refuse, potatoes and everything of that kind, while in Canada we compel the distiller to adopt a very high standard. The foreign distiller has an advantage any way because he can manufacture cheaper than the Canadian, and the very fact that his liquor is imported gives it an additional value, the consumer paying the duty. Will the minister investigate this, and may we expect any reform in the immediate future?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The importation of Scotch or any other whisky does not come within the province of the Inland Revenue Department. The Customs Department deals with it.
You should not allow the Minister of Customs to encroach on you, to run in his stuff in opposition to yours.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It is quite true that the alcohol made in Canada is matured for two years before it is permitted to be sold. That regulation was made many years ago, I believe at the request of the manufacturers of alcohol in Canada. I do not know the motive in making it; it may improve the quality of the whisky. This requirement is maintained because the distillery men wish it, not because the department is particularly anxious to continue the two year period of maturing. We have no control over the manufacture of whisky in Scotland. There would, however, appear to be an unfair competition when liquor a month old from Scotland competes with Canadian liquor kept in bond for two years to mature. I do not know whether the Canadian is any better than the other; although I have sampled both, I am not a judge. I freely admit that there is an apparent hardship upon the Canadian distillers, but they have never made any representations to the department in that regard. Within the last month or two the compounders have made certain representations regarding labelling and mixing. Certain features of the question are now under consideration of the department. My hon. friend will see that the Excise Department has nothing whatever to do with imposing any conditions upon liquor imported into Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

Is it the policy of the government to superannuate men who can still work, or men who have done service and cannot work any longer? If this gentleman has been superannuated, how is it Mr. TEMPLEMAN.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This is the usual vote.
How much is expended in British Columbia for salaries of inspectors and others?

speechtext: The amount is very little indeed. The inspectors of foods are officers of the department, who are appointed at very small sums, ranging from $100 to $200 and in some cases $300. Is one inspector in Vancouver sufficient?

speechtext: One might do for the whole province.

Is the minister aware that the amount of milk alone sold in the city of Vancouver would require the services of five inspectors? Does he know anything about the prosecutions for the adulteration of milk in Vancouver?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The Department of Inland Revenue, under the Adulteration of Foods Act, has nothing to do with the prosecution of people for the selling of impure milk. That is a municipal matter. There is scarcely a city in the Dominion which has not by-laws in that connection and inspectors, and the department does not infringe upon municipal jurisdiction.
Where do the municipalities get their power to pass their by-laws with regard to the adulteration of milk?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: In the Adulteration of Foods Act.
In what section?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I cannot say offhand but my bon. friend is a lawyer and must know. Every municipality has the power to appoint inspectors, and many have done it.
I would have thought that as the subject has been dealt with here, the jurisdiction would be vested in this parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Under clause 10 of the Adulteration of Foods Act, municipalities may appoint inspectors, but even in addition to that, if I remember rightly, the municipalities can protect themselves. They have jurisdiction with regard to hygienic conditions in dairy establishments and stables and that sort of thing, and I am inclined to think that, under the provincial law, the municipalities can be delegated that power. However, I would not care to enter into a legal controversy with my hon. friend who for years has been the solicitor for the municipality of the city of Vancouver. I would refer him also to section 13 of the Adulteration of Foods Act, which gives further power of the same kind.

I do not seek to enter into a legal discussion with the minister, but am merely drawing his attention to the fact that the machinery of the Act is exceedingly cumbersome. Not only is tire substantive part of the Act insufficient to protect the public, but the machinery is inadequate and complicated. I was going to suggest that it would be desirable to fix a standard for milk and that the machinery of the Act should be improved, because at present it is impossible to get a conviction under it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am disposed to agree with my hon. friend that the Act can be^ improved, and I think that the first thing to do is to provide a standard. If we had a fixed standard for all food stuffs, we could enforce the Act much more effectively. That is a matter the department has under consideration.

I am suggesting not only that the department should fix the standard, blit that it should improve the machinery of the Act. For instance, the public, in order to reach the halls of justice, must go through the portals of your inspectors.

The minister comes before us this year, as in other years, and asks for money which, as at present used, is wasted or worse than wasted. He pays his inspectors to go about the country and buy samples of various articles. These samples are sent to Ottawa and analysed, and the results are published in a bulletin. The bulletin shows that three-quarters of these articles are adulterated. Yet no body is prosecuted, because there is no standard and the minister will not fix a standard. Practically every family in this country is using adulterated foods which are sold in the stores generally. The minister knows this, for the facts are before



him in his own bulletin. But it is the same old story-they have not fixed the standard and we cannot enforce the Act. I hold that we should not vote another dollar for this service until the minister says that any man who sells adulterated food will be prosecuted by the officers of the department.

There are two things absolutely necessary in order to make that Act workable; one is the fixing of a standard and the other is the taking away from the inspectors of the power to shelter the guilty. I am not charging that they actually shelter the guilty, but what I do say is that the public cannot go directly into the courts and secure the enforcement of the Act except under onerous conditions. If these were changed, the machinery would be more workable.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I think the results of the analyses of the collection made all over the country and the publication of the results have been good. The publicity thus given to the facts and also the prosecutions that have taken place and the imposition of penalties, so far as they have been imposed, have had a very good effect upon the purity of food-stuffs actuallysold in Canada. I have here a memorandum showing the percentage of adulteration for ten years past, and in every case there is a considerable reduction in the percentage. For instance, in maple sugar the percentage of adulteration went down from 45 per cent in 1905 to 13 per cent in 1908; in maple syrup from 82 per cent to 13 per cent in the same period. In milk, the percentage below standard in 1890 was 22 per cent. It has varied year by year, going down as low as three or four per cent, but last year it was ten per cent. I have another memorandum showing the results of the analysis of a number of samples covering a very large variety of articles. I will not weary the House by reading it, but I may say that the result is exceedingly encouraging indeed, there being a far less percentage of adulteration in all lines to-day than there was even five years ago. I think this good result is, in a measure at all events, due to the enforcement of the Adulteration of Foods Act through the collection of samples and the publication of the bulletins.

the department has incurred up to the present time, we will not prosecute.

These amounts are the amounts that the department offered to accept in lieu of prosecuting. We thought then and think still that the penalty then imposed was quite sufficient. There is still in the Justice Department a large number of cases {or prosecution.

That is the mystery of the case, why these amounts were paid. A man is guilty of selling adulterated food, that is, he has committed an offence, not against the department but against the public, and an analysis is made at the expense of the government inspector. The accused is brought up; some times he is brought before the man who has the patronage in the district, and sometimes to the inspector; he is brought up, and that is all. He is told: Now, if you pay the analyst so much, and the lawyer that is engaged in the matter so much, we will hush it up. Now, the minister has failed to show any cases of conviction. Again, if the minister wishes to make that Act useful, let him call on his department to do away with the machinery which puts the guilty man in the power of the inspector. I am not charging that any particular inspector has abused that power, but I come very near it, and I say that the figures the minister has read out show that these men, guilty of a crime against the public, are brought, not into the courts of justice-the only place where justice 43i
can be done to the public in case of an offence against the public-but into the office of some good Liberal lawyer, or bad Liberal lawyer, if you will; and he is told that if he will fork out $5, say to the analyst, and something to the lawyer, and something for somebody else, amounting perhaps to $82, as the minister says in one case, why, he can go scot free. The crime is condoned in the lawyer's office, not in court, fior he never gets there. That is our experience all over Canada, at least on the coast, that this Act is not workable. The inspector has to shove his face into the prosecution, he is charged with the duty of enforcing the Act, and instead of chasing the guilty man into court, he chases into some private office and settles with him. I submit again that the minister has proven by his own figures that the machinery of that Act is in bad need of amendment. I would ask the minister if he has any cases of conviction?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Yes, lots of them. I think my hon. friend is not as familiar with the mode of procedure under the Adulteration of Food Act as he ought to be. The inspector, who has been roundly abused by my hon. friend as shielding the guilty, has little or nothing to do with the enforcement of the Adulteration of Food Act. As a matter of fact, I have always thought that the title of inspector

of food is a misnomer. Under the Adulteration of Food Act the inspector is simply a clerk in the excise office, and receives from us a small salary, $100 or $200 a year in addition to his regular salary for the purpose of collecting samples, when he is advised by the chief chemist. lie goes to a grocery store, or any other place, and he buys a sample, and divides it into three parts. He seals these in the presence of the dealer, leaves one sample with the dealer, and sends another to the head office in Ottawa. That is all he has to do; he is a witness, therefore, that that narticular article was bought from that particular grocer. He puts his seal on it ; and the sample sent here is analysed. Now, the inspector disappears altogether from the scene until there is a prosecution, when he js a witness to this fact only, that this is the sample of the butter, it may be, ot the pepper, or whatever article that he bought from that particular dealer; that is all he has to do. He does not initiate proceedings, he has nothing to do with the prosecution, he has nothing to do with the settlement. The department in Ottawa, after these samples are analysed and adulteration is found to exist, places the matter in the hands of the Justice Department, and from that time until a settlement is reached the Inland Revenue Department has nothing more to do with the matter. My hon. friend has been unfair in his reflections upon the inspectors. They	are	our	agents simplyfor the purpose of collecting samples for analvsis. I	am	free	to admit	thatthe Adulteration	of	Food	Act needs	improvement, and	I	hope we will	improve it. Certainly the first thing to do is to provide a standard of food, so we will not fail. One reason why in the last few years we have not prosecuted to a finish as much as we formerly tried to do, and why we accept the payment of the expenses of the department rather than go on and prosecute, is because in a prosecution, I think in the city Of Montreal, the judge refused to convict because there was no standard. I imagine that another judge -would follow that precedent and refuse to convict where there was no standard. I do not know that there is any more information I can give my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Cowan). I have said frankly that I think the Adulteration of Food Act ought to be improved, and I trust will be improved this session.

Will the minister go further and admit that it is not a desirable mode of enforcing that Act that I, for instance, who might wish to prosecute for a.n offence under the Act, would have to Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
go to the inspector and make a deposit of $25.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: My hon. friend cannot do that under the present Act. The inspector has nothing to do with that and never received a deposit, as far as I am aware.
A deposit is required in certain cases under the Act before a private individual can prosecute.

The Act provides that if upon analysis an article is found to be adulterated the person at whose instance the analysis is made may prosecute the offender upon making a deposit of $25 with the collector of Inland Revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is not the inspector.

It is the same thing, you have said that the officers of your department are your inspectors. . It works out in the same way; I cannot get a prosecution unless I put up security. Rut if you commit a common law offence, an assault, I can lay an information and prosecute you. why is the distinction made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The clause referred to is a provision whereby any person can prosecute, and I think that the provision requiring a deposit is very proper. Where there is adulteration the department carries on prosecutions and has done so to a very large extent, but there is also that provision that if a private individual desires to prosecute by making the deposit, I presume to cover the preliminary expenses, he is privileged to do so. While the provision is a proper one, I do not think it has been taken advantage of by any person.

I take issue with the minister there, any man who has to do with the actual business of prosecuting offenders would disagree with him. As that Act is framed it is in the mind of the public that they have nothing to do with the enforcement of the Act. It is in the hands of the government and the local heelers are quick to catch on to that and get out of it whatever fees they can, so that there is a settlement and no conviction. I doubt if there could be a conviction because there is no fixed standard, but even if you had a standard the prosecution would lose its way in some government office and the case would never reach the court under that provision because there is an embargo placed on the public prosecuting under that Act.
Mr. 0. A. WILSON. There may be something in what the hon. member has said about the framing of this Act in relation to prosecutions. I have had some experi-

ence as an attorney in the city of Montreal. The hon. member has asked for cases of conviction. In 1906 or 1907 when the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Brodeur) held the portfolio of Inland Revenue, I was charged by this government to prosecute in five cases of adulteration, three of maple syrup, and two of butter. In the maple syrup prosecutions I secured three convictions and the defendants were fined $20. There was doubt in the mind of the magistrate about the working of the Act, especially in the absence of a Canadian standard. We acted upon an American standard and another provision of the Act under which we had to refer to a pharmacopeia, French or British, I do not remember exactly. Mr. Small, who was prosecuted, appealed to the Court of Appeal, criminal side. The case was argued before Mr. Justice Tren-holme, who kept it en delibere for a year; the appeal was allowed, the conviction quashed and a report made to the government to that effect. If I remember the argument advanced by Mr. Cotton, a very able lawyer for the defence, he objected to the provision of the law that the' certificate of the analysis is prima facie evidence that has to be rebutted by the person accused. He also based his argument on the absence of a standard. After consultation with the gentleman who was acting as chief analyst in Ottawa just after the death of Mr. Macfarlane, we came to the conclusion that in order to do justice to the people of our community, many samples of maple syrup would have to be gathered from different points. In order to make it uniform or perhaps have different standards according to the different soil, land, or maple trees in the different provinces. The other two cases in which I was engaged were cases of the sale of oleomargarine. Both of the accused were found guilty and fined $20 and costs. So I am glad to be in a position to inform my hon. friend (Mr. Cowan) that convictions were secured. I think the department concluded that some amendment should be brought into force, which would make the Act more -workable.-As to the adulteration of milk, my hon. friend is aware that we have special legislation in Quebec which empowers the different towns and cities to pass by-laws on this question. The city of Montreal, for instance, has passed a by-law and almost daily in the report of the recorder's court you read items in the campaign against these offenders, against any Act, federal, provincial or municipal. They are very severely prosecuted and I do not see any reason to complain of the working of this Act. My impression is that the clause quoted by my hon. friend which enables the municipalities to take advantage of this Act, offers to those communities which are not populous enough to have a city char
ter an opportunity to pass by-laws for the proper inspection of the articles of food that are sold to the public.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wilson) cannot cite a single case in which a private individual has been prosecuted to conviction, and he admits that in the absence of a fixed standard the Act is practically ineffective. The fact is that the Dominion government is playing dog in the manger. This statute does not fix the standard and should the provincial government legislate along the same lines and a prosecution be entered under the Dominion statute then the courts would say that the federal parliament having already exercised jurisdiction the provincial Act is ultra vires. This proves beyond doubt that the fixing of a standard by Dominion statute is an absolute necessity.
Does this item cover the expense of the analysis of the samples of food and of the fertilizers sent in for registration under the Act of last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: When samples are sent in for registration they have already been analysed by the manufacturers, but this will cover the expense of the samples sent in by the people to be analysed at the laboratory.
What progress is being made in the registration under the Act of last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Very good progress. I think most of the manufacturers are registered now and the Act will go into force by the first of the year.

The minister told us that when these samples are analysed and found adulterated he hands the case over to the Department of Justice. It seems to me that that is the end of it. I would like to know any manufacturer who has been prosecuted in connection with these adulterated food stuffs that are bought in the grocery stores.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: When the chemist finishes his analysis and adulterations are found the case is sent to the Department of Justice as the hon. gentleman says.

And that is apparently the end of it, because I have never heard of a case where the manufacturer or the seller of adulterated food has been prosecuted. It is time that the law should be put in force. It is all nonsense to hand the case over to the Department of Justice and let it remain hung up there when the proper course would be to institute these prosecutions at once and stop the sale of these adulterated articles.
Salaries, weights and measures inspection. $76,000.
What revenue is received from the inspection of weights and measures?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

speechtext: Sometimes people complain that they are charged too much for this inspection. What charges have the inspectors a right to make?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: There is a fixed tariff established by order in council.
Are the self-computing scales now so generally in use subject to the inspection of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: All scales that are used for buying and selling must be inspected.
Is the inspector allowed to charge for the cartage of the weights from the store to the station or wherever he is going to make the test and bank again?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We pay all transportation charges, but the cartage charges from one store to another are borne pro rata by the different parties whose scales are inspected.

I am informed that there are a great many self-computing scales in use in the country that have not been inspected by the department. I assume that a specially trained officer would be required to make a proper inspection of scales of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

speechtext: I understand that the law is that if you own the meter you have to pay for the inspection, but if you rent the meter the company that rents it to you pays for the inspection. Is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.
I would suggest that the law be changed to make the company pay for all the inspections.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is the owner of the meter, whether a company or a private individual, who pays for the inspection.

That is not fair to the consumer, because he buys the meter from the company.
Rent, fuel, travelling expenses, postage, stationery, &e., for gas and electric light inspection and the purchase and repairs of instruments, $25,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This is an increase of $4,000, due to the increasing number of plants all over the country. Every small town now is having its own electric light, and the expense of inspection has increased considerably. We employ only qualified electricians as inspectors.
Inspection of export of electric power, $1,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The chief electric inspector has to proceed to places where electric power is generated and make an inspection and report. He made an inspection, for instance, and spent considerable time at FoTt Francis and also at Niagara Falls.
Do we get any revenue from this?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The only revenue we get is the $50 license paid by the companies that export electricity.
Why should the government look after the export of electrical power without getting some profit?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We have had the Act several years and do not get any profit out of it.
These are private companies engaged in the business, and we should charge them sufficient license to cover the expense of administering the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I imagine that the object of the Act is, if deemed advisable, to restrict the export of elecric power or at all events to regulate it. We have it within cur power to give permission to export or refuse that permission, as we think best in the public interest. It is necessary that cur chief inspector should visit the different places and see what power is being developed and how much exported. We have to administer the Act and pay the expenses of adminisetering it.

TAY'LOR. We ought to charge a higher license so that the Act will be self-sustaining and not be a drag on the country. These private companies are making money, and we certainly should make them pay a sufficient license to meet expenses. How often has the inspector to visit these places where the power-is exported?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: At least once a year.
TAY'LOR. And does that cost $1,500?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No, we did not spend quite a thousand dollars last year.
Why then ask for $1,500?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The expense next year may be a little more than last.
Did it cost $1,000 to send an inspector once to these two places, Fort Francis and Niagara Falls?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: And New Brunswick.
How long was he at each place? Did each of these three visits cost $300?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am told that it took about a month altogether to make the trips.
He is paid a salary as well, and this is for expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, purely expenses.
And that officer spends $900 on travelling expenses in one month?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The deputy minister informs me that he made a trip to London, England, to attend the international convention of electricians, and the expenses of that trip were charged to this item.

What right had the minister to send an inspector to England and charge his expenses against this item? He should ask for a special vote or take it out of miscellaneous expenses. In any event there is no need to vote $1,500 this year unless the minister contemplates giving him another trip to the old country.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We could get along with $1,000 if it were worth while changing the estimate.

If the minister took a sum of money and 'gave an officer a trip to England unauthorized by parliament, we ought not to trust him with $1,500. If we deduct the trip to England, $100 each should pay the expenses to these three places.	'	.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The chief electrical engineer who attended the convention in London, was authorized to do so by order in council. It was a very important convention for the purpose of fixiug the standard electrical union.

It was all right to send him there for information, but he was not sent there in connection with the export of electrical power and his expenses should be charged to some other vote. The minister admits that his expenses will cost some $200 or $300 and is asking $1,500. The item should be Tedueed to $500 That surely should pay the cost of visiting three places in the year, one trip to each place. He is asking for money which he does not know how to spend unless by giving some officer a trip to England and charging the expenses to this vote. The council had no right to authorize this man to go to England and charge his expenses to a vote when the House did not agree to it. I move that the item be reduced to $500.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I frankly admit that after the explanation given me by the deputy minister and the chief electrical engineer, $1,000 will do.
Inland Revenue Department-minor revenues, $500
Interior Department - ordnance lands -
salaries and expenses, $1,655.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: These minor revenues are collections, such as administering the Ferries Act, advertising for tenders for ferries, and printing law stamps to be used in the Yukon. The other item does not concern the Inland Revenue Department, that is revenue collected by the Interior Department.	.
Why are these two items mixed up?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I cannot explain as to the Interior Department, it is only one of the minor revenues.

The Minister of the Interior should make an explanation of this item. .1 do not see why the items should be mixed in this way, charging part of the expenditure of the Interior Department to the Inland Revenue Department. We had better separate them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This vote has been taken for years, these items have been bracketted together, and I do not think either of them was ever discussed before.
We would like to know what this money was spent for, and the Minister of the Interior is not here to tell us.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
Then we will have to let it stand.
Customs-salaries and contingent expenses of the several ports in the Dominion, including pay for overtime of officers, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $1,875,-
000.

Now I appeal to the Minister of Finance, we have done a good day's work, and it is time to adjourn. Both the leader of the opposition and the ex-minister of finance are absent, and there are very few members in the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the absence of these gentlemen indicates that they were content to let things run.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: This is an increase-
I appeal to the Minister of Finance that it is time to adjourn.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: When my hon. friend is present, nothing -will go through that should not go through. We have our officers here now, and it would be very inconvenient to if we were obliged to bring them here another day.

We have done a fair day's work, and owing to the absence of the leader of the opposition and the exMinister of Finance who is out of the country, I do not think that we should be asked to vote this large sum.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: If these items don't go .through to-night they will have to wait until January.

You don't require this money until after the 31st of March. I again appeal to the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Labour has advocated an eight hour day for the government service, and we have already passed the limit.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: We have only passed three items to-day. But if the hon. gentleman will say that the leader of the opposition and the ex-Minister of Finance wish to be present why of course we shall have to wait.	*
I say that the exMinister of Finance wants to be present for all the items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In that case, if my hon. friend is determined not to go on with the public business, I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Some resolutions reported.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
First annual report of the Civil Service Commission.-Mr. Murphy.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.	.
If we get through private members business on Monday, will the government go on with the estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will continue with the ministers who were on the programme this evening for estimates.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11 p.m.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Monday, December 13, 1909.
